lessons.title: Sanctions as a Weapon: How They Work and Who Actually Gets Hit

body.text: Sanctions are designed to hurt the country that misbehaves. In practice, they often hurt the sanctioning country's own businesses, the target's ordinary citizens, and third countries like India who suddenly have to navigate a market with fewer buyers, cheaper sellers, and real compliance risk in between.

children.text: Sanctions are economic and financial restrictions one country, or a coalition of countries, imposes on another, or on specific individuals and companies, to pressure a change in behaviour without going to war. They have become one of the most frequently used geopolitical tools of the last decade, and they create some of the most direct, tradeable market effects of any weapon covered in this course, from oil price discounts to banking sector volatility. India, as a large energy importer that trades with almost everyone, sits closer to the middle of this story than most investors realise.

cells: Bans or restricts specific imports or exports
Restrictions on exporting advanced technology to a sanctioned country
Freezes assets or cuts access to the international banking system
Freezing a country's central bank reserves held abroad, or removing banks from SWIFT messaging
Targets an entire industry rather than the whole economy
Restrictions specifically on a country's energy, defence, or financial sector
Targets specific people or companies directly
Freezing the personal assets of officials or business figures tied to a sanctioned government
Threatens penalties on third-country firms that keep dealing with the sanctioned party
A foreign bank facing US restrictions for processing payments linked to a sanctioned entity, even with no direct US connection

children.text: Case Study Snapshot: Sanctions on Russia Since 2022

stats.label: SWIFT exclusion
stats.context: Cut off from SWIFT's international payment messaging system from March 2022, though some banks handling energy payments were initially left connected

stats.label: Frozen reserves
stats.context: Approximate value of Russian central bank foreign reserves frozen by Western jurisdictions, widely reported as one of the largest asset freezes of a sovereign country in history

stats.label: G7 oil price cap
stats.context: A cap on seaborne Russian crude, effective from December 2022, enforced by denying Western insurance and shipping services to cargoes sold above it

children.text: The Price Cap and India's Discounted Oil Trade

The G7 price cap was designed to let Russian oil keep flowing globally, avoiding a supply shock, while limiting how much revenue Russia could earn from it. Its real-world effect was different from its intent: Russian crude simply sold to willing non-Western buyers at a steep discount to global benchmark prices. India was the biggest beneficiary of this. Indian crude imports from Russia went from a negligible share before 2022 to reportedly somewhere between a third and 40 percent of India's total crude imports in the years since, making Russia India's single largest source of crude oil, a dramatic reversal from a relationship that barely registered before the war.

body.text: This is a direct, tradeable consequence of a sanctions regime: Indian refiners including Reliance, IOC, BPCL, and HPCL have benefited from cheaper Russian crude feedstock, supporting refining margins even as the broader geopolitical backdrop stayed tense. A sanctions story elsewhere in the world quietly became an Indian refining sector earnings story.

children.text: Who Actually Gets Hit: The Shadow Fleet and Evasion

Sanctioned countries rarely just accept the restriction, they build around it. A well-documented response to the oil price cap has been the growth of a 'shadow fleet', older tankers operating outside mainstream Western insurance and flagging systems, allowing cargoes to move and be sold above the price cap without directly using sanctioned Western services. This raises real questions for every country buying that oil, including India, about compliance risk, insurance coverage in the event of an accident, and the possibility of secondary sanctions if enforcement priorities shift. India has generally maintained that it does not consider itself bound by sanctions it has not itself adopted through the UN framework, and has continued sourcing oil it judges to be commercially available, but the compliance landscape around this trade remains genuinely complex and can change with little warning.

body.title: Intended Effect vs What Often Happens

columns.label: What sanctions are meant to do
points: Cut off funding or resources for the targeted behaviour
Pressure a change in policy without military conflict
Isolate the target economically and diplomatically

columns.label: What often happens instead
points: The target reroutes trade toward willing partners, often at a discount, rather than stopping the activity
Third countries and their companies absorb both new opportunity and new compliance risk
Policy change, when it happens at all, tends to take years, not months, and is rarely the sanctions' effect alone

body.title: Reading a New Sanctions Headline
body.scenario: A country is hit with a new round of financial sanctions, including removal of its largest banks from SWIFT. Within weeks, reports emerge that its oil exports to two large Asian economies, including India, are rising sharply, at a discount to global prices.
body.prompt: Is this outcome consistent with how sanctions have historically played out, based on this lesson? What would you expect to happen to the Indian refining sector's margins as a result?
body.modelAnswer: Yes, this is a very consistent pattern, sanctions rarely stop trade entirely, they tend to redirect it toward willing buyers at a discount, as seen with Russian oil and India after 2022. For Indian refiners, cheaper discounted crude feedstock would likely support refining margins, similar to the pattern this lesson described, though an investor should also watch for compliance risk and the possibility of secondary sanctions pressure if enforcement priorities shift later.

body.title: Naming the Sanction Type
body.question: A government freezes the personal bank accounts and travel privileges of a handful of specific business executives tied to a foreign regime, without restricting that country's broader trade. This is an example of:
body.explanation: Targeting specific named individuals or companies, rather than an entire industry, country, or third-party firms dealing with the target, is the defining feature of individual and entity sanctions.

cards.definition: The global messaging network banks use to instruct and confirm international payments. Removal from SWIFT does not freeze money directly, but makes cross-border payments far slower and harder to execute.

A sanctions mechanism that limits how much a buyer can pay for a sanctioned commodity while still using Western insurance and shipping services, designed to keep supply flowing globally while capping the seller's revenue.
Tankers, often older vessels, operating outside mainstream Western insurance and flagging systems, used to move sanctioned oil cargoes and sell them above a price cap.
Penalties threatened against third-country companies or banks that continue doing business with a sanctioned entity, even without a direct connection to the sanctioning country.

points: Sanctions come in five main forms: trade, financial, sectoral, individual or entity, and secondary sanctions, each targeting a different part of an economy or its relationships
The sanctions regime on Russia since 2022 included SWIFT exclusion for select banks, an approximate $300 billion central bank reserve freeze, and a $60 per barrel price cap on seaborne oil

The price cap redirected, rather than stopped, Russian oil flows; India became a major buyer of discounted Russian crude, reportedly making up somewhere between a third and 40 percent of its total crude imports in the years after 2022
This directly benefited Indian oil marketing and refining companies through cheaper feedstock and stronger refining margins, a clear example of a sanctions story becoming an Indian earnings story

Sanctions are frequently evaded through mechanisms like the shadow fleet, and third countries buying the affected commodity face real, evolving compliance and secondary sanctions risk, even when their own government does not consider itself bound by the sanctions

body.text: Figures on frozen reserves, price caps, and India's Russian crude import share are approximate, widely reported estimates that can shift as policy and trade patterns evolve. This lesson references specific companies and countries for educational, factual illustration only, and is not a recommendation regarding any company, country, or trade. Sanctions compliance is a genuinely complex legal area; this lesson is not legal or compliance advice.
